subject: Regnal ages and reign lengths of Judah's last kings, Babylonian exile, and Cyrus decree

figures.name: Jehoahaz — age at accession
figures.note: All three traditions agree on Jehoahaz's accession age of 23 years (2 Chr 36:2); no textual dispute.

figures.name: Jehoahaz — reign length (months)
figures.note: Three-month reign of Jehoahaz is universally attested across all textual witnesses.

figures.name: Jehoiakim — age at accession
figures.note: Jehoiakim's accession age of 25 is consistently attested; harmonizes with 2 Kings 23:36.

figures.name: Jehoiakim — reign length (years)
figures.note: Eleven-year reign of Jehoiakim is consistent across all textual traditions.

figures.name: Jehoiachin — age at accession
figures.note: The LXX reads 18 years (harmonizing with 2 Kings 24:8), while MT and SP read 8; this is one of the most debated divergences in the Chronicler's text, likely reflecting a scribal confusion of the Hebrew letters chet (8) and yod-chet (18), or a deliberate harmonization in LXX toward the Kings parallel.

figures.name: Jehoiachin — reign length (months)
figures.note: Three-month reign is uniformly attested; the parallel in 2 Kings 24:8 adds 'ten days' but the Chronicles text is consistent internally.

figures.name: Zedekiah — age at accession
figures.note: Zedekiah's accession age of 21 is consistent across all textual traditions.

figures.name: Zedekiah — reign length (years)
figures.note: Eleven-year reign of Zedekiah is universally attested.

figures.name: Duration of Babylonian exile / land sabbath (years)
figures.note: The 70-year figure for the Babylonian exile sabbath rest is consistent across all traditions (2 Chr 36:21), reflecting Jeremiah 25:11-12 and 29:10.

figures.name: Cyrus's regnal year of decree
figures.note: The first year of Cyrus as the frame for the restoration decree is universally attested.

systematic_analysis.pattern: Unlike the Pentateuchal patriarchal chronologies where MT, LXX, and SP display systematic arithmetic offsets (typically +100 years in LXX for pre-Flood patriarchs, or -2 years in SP), the divergences in 2 Chronicles 36 are isolated rather than systematic. The sole significant numerical divergence — Jehoiachin's accession age of 8 (MT/SP) versus 18 (LXX) — is a single-figure anomaly that can be fully explained by either a graphic confusion between ח (8) and יח (18) in Hebrew, or by the LXX translator's tendency to harmonize toward the parallel in 2 Kings 24:8 (which reads 18 in both MT and LXX). No consistent arithmetic transformation rule (addition, subtraction, or multiplication) connects the three traditions across the chapter as a whole.
systematic_analysis.pattern_plain: Almost all the numbers in 2 Chronicles 36 are the same in all three Bible versions — the only real difference is one number about King Jehoiachin's age, where one version says 8 and another says 18, and that single discrepancy is most likely a copying mistake or a deliberate correction to match another Bible book.

theories.name: Scribal Error (Graphic/Paleographic Confusion)
theories.summary: The divergence between MT/SP '8' and LXX '18' for Jehoiachin's accession age is most parsimoniously explained by paleographic confusion in the Hebrew script. In ancient Hebrew numeral notation, the numeral 8 (ח) could be confused with 18 (י״ח or written out as שמונה עשרה), and in the Vorlage tradition the digit-word or letter could have been misread. Jack Finegan's 'Handbook of Biblical Chronology' extensively documents how single-digit discrepancies in regnal ages are among the most common categories of scribal transmission error, particularly when a scribe's exemplar used archaic or cursive letterforms. The fact that 2 Kings 24:8 independently attests 18 (in both MT and LXX of Kings) strengthens the scribal-error hypothesis: a copyist of Chronicles, aware of the Kings parallel, may have 'corrected' 8 to 18, or the original Chronicles figure was 18 and was corrupted to 8.
theories.summary_plain: The most likely explanation is a simple copying mistake — the number 8 and the number 18 look similar enough in ancient Hebrew writing that a scribe could easily mix them up, and other ancient manuscripts of a related Bible book (2 Kings) say 18, supporting the idea that one version was accidentally changed.
supporting_evidence: 2 Kings 24:8 reads 18 in both MT and LXX, making an 8-year-old king in Chronicles appear anomalous against the parallel tradition.
Paleographic analysis by scholars including F.M. Cross demonstrates that numerical notations in archaic and square Hebrew scripts are among the most corruption-prone elements in scribal transmission.
Jack Finegan ('Handbook of Biblical Chronology,' rev. ed. 1998, pp. 103-110) catalogs single-digit regnal age discrepancies as a distinct, recurrent error class in Chronicles-Kings parallels.
The Septuagint's consistent rendering of 18 across Chronicles and Kings suggests it drew on a Hebrew Vorlage that already read 18, or the LXX translator harmonized to the Kings parallel.

The SP and MT agreement on 8 in Chronicles could reflect preservation of a deliberately distinct Chronicler's theological perspective (an 8-year-old king emphasizing divine sovereignty), but is more simply explained as a shared error in the proto-MT/SP tradition.
weaknesses: If the original Chronicles reading was 18 (harmonized with Kings), the origin of the MT/SP '8' requires a separate corruption hypothesis, creating a two-step error scenario.

Some scholars (e.g., Sara Japhet, 'I & II Chronicles,' OTL) argue the Chronicler may have deliberately used different numbers from Kings for theological reasons, which would make 'scribal error' an oversimplification.
The theory cannot fully account for why SP and MT agree on the anomalous '8' rather than the Kings-consistent '18' if copying from a shared error-free tradition.

theories.name: LXX Harmonization Toward Kings Parallel
theories.summary: The LXX reading of 18 for Jehoiachin's accession age may not reflect a superior Vorlage but rather a translator's deliberate harmonization toward the 2 Kings 24:8 parallel, which reads 18 in all traditions. Emanuel Tov's work on LXX translation technique ('The Text-Critical Use of the Septuagint,' 3rd ed.) identifies harmonization to parallel passages as a systematic feature of certain LXX translators, particularly in Chronicles where the translator demonstrably cross-referenced Kings. The LXX of Chronicles (Greek: Paralipomenon) is known to be a relatively free translation with harmonizing tendencies, making it plausible that the Greek translator encountered '8' in his Hebrew Vorlage and adjusted it to '18' based on the Kings parallel rather than reflecting an independent textual tradition.
theories.summary_plain: The Greek translation (LXX) may have simply 'corrected' the number 8 to 18 to make it match the same story in another Bible book (2 Kings), rather than reflecting an actually older or better manuscript.
supporting_evidence: The LXX of Paralipomenon (Chronicles) is documented by scholars including Curtis and Madsen ('ICC Chronicles,' 1910) as exhibiting frequent harmonizations to the Kings parallel narratives.
Emanuel Tov's typology of LXX translation techniques includes 'harmonization to context and parallel passages' as a major category, well-attested in the historical books.

The absence of any other numerical divergence in 2 Chronicles 36 between LXX and MT/SP makes a systematic independent textual tradition implausible; the single adjustment to 18 is more consistent with targeted harmonization.

The Göttingen Septuagint critical apparatus for Paralipomenon confirms no significant variant support for a reading other than 18 in the Greek manuscript tradition, suggesting a unified LXX harmonization rather than a divergent Vorlage.
weaknesses: If the LXX Vorlage already read 18 in Hebrew (as some scholars argue), the harmonization happened at the Vorlage stage, not in the Greek translation itself, making this a Vorlage issue rather than a translation issue.
The theory assumes the MT/SP reading of 8 is original to Chronicles, which remains contested given the Kings parallel.
LXX harmonization theory does not explain why the MT/SP would preserve a chronologically awkward reading (8-year-old king acting autonomously) if the 'correct' reading of 18 was widely known.

theories.name: Independent Textual Traditions
theories.summary: A minority view holds that the divergence between MT/SP (8) and LXX (18) for Jehoiachin's accession age reflects genuinely independent textual traditions — that the Chronicler's source tradition independently preserved a different number from the Kings tradition, and the LXX Vorlage preserved the Kings-aligned figure while the proto-MT/SP preserved the Chronicler's distinctive figure. Jeremy Sexton's analysis of textual divergences emphasizes that not all numerical discrepancies between MT and LXX reduce to scribal error or harmonization; some reflect divergent compositional histories. However, in 2 Chronicles 36 specifically, the total absence of systematic divergence across all other figures in the chapter makes the independent-traditions hypothesis weak — the single anomaly is more economically explained by error or harmonization than by positing two genuinely independent source streams for one number.
theories.summary_plain: Some scholars think the different numbers come from two genuinely separate ancient versions of the text that were never the same, but in this chapter the evidence for that is weak because everything else agrees perfectly.
supporting_evidence: Jeremy Sexton and Henry Green's methodology ('Who Was Born When Elisha Lost His Hair?', Westminster Theological Journal) advocates treating numerical divergences as potential evidence of independent source traditions before invoking error.

The Chronicler demonstrably drew on sources independent of the Kings tradition in numerous places, making it theoretically possible that an independent source tradition carried a different age for Jehoiachin.

The Qumran biblical manuscripts (4QChr) provide limited but real evidence that the Chronicles text had variant forms in the Second Temple period, supporting the possibility of genuine tradition divergence.
weaknesses: The complete agreement of all other figures in 2 Chronicles 36 across MT, LXX, and SP makes an independent tradition hypothesis for a single number methodologically unjustified by parsimony.

The independent traditions theory provides no explanation for why the LXX tradition would independently arrive at exactly the same number (18) as the Kings tradition rather than a third distinct figure.
Without manuscript evidence from Chronicles traditions predating the LXX that read 18, the theory remains speculative.

theories.name: Theological Motivation (MT/SP Distinctive Theology)
theories.summary: A small number of commentators, including Sara Japhet and William Johnstone, have proposed that the Chronicler's use of '8' for Jehoiachin's age (contra Kings' '18') may reflect a theological or rhetorical purpose — emphasizing the king's youth and incapacity as a divine judgment motif, or deliberately distancing the Chronicler's narrative from the Kings parallel. However, theological motivation theories for numerical divergences in Chronicles are generally weakly supported because the Chronicler shows no consistent pattern of age-modification for theological effect elsewhere in chapter 36 or across the book. Henry Green's work on systematic theological deflation in the MT Pentateuch (as a Second Temple polemic against Samaritan chronology) provides a methodological framework for theological motivation, but that framework applies to systematic, mathematically coherent patterns — not to the isolated single-figure anomaly seen here.
theories.summary_plain: A few scholars think the number 8 was chosen deliberately to make a theological point about the young king's helplessness, but there is no consistent pattern of this kind of theological number-changing across the rest of the chapter, so this explanation is not very convincing.
supporting_evidence: The Chronicler's narrative in 2 Chr 36:9-10 is notably compressed compared to 2 Kings 24:8-17, suggesting a different theological agenda that could theoretically extend to numerical presentation.
Sara Japhet ('I & II Chronicles,' OTL, 1993) acknowledges the possibility that the Chronicler worked from independent source material with different numbers rather than mechanically copying Kings.
weaknesses: No consistent pattern of theologically motivated age modification exists elsewhere in 2 Chronicles 36 or across the Chronicler's regnal summaries that would support this as a deliberate technique.
The theological motivation hypothesis is unfalsifiable in this case without corroborating structural or thematic evidence from the surrounding text.
Henry Green and Jeremy Sexton's methodology requires systematic, mathematically regular patterns as a precondition for invoking theological motivation — a criterion not met by this single divergence.
The Chronicler's abbreviated treatment of Jehoiachin (only 2 verses) provides insufficient context to distinguish theological purpose from transmission error.

theories.name: SP Harmonization
theories.summary: The Samaritan Pentateuch is not a relevant textual witness for 2 Chronicles 36 since Chronicles is not part of the Samaritan biblical canon; therefore, SP harmonization as a theory does not apply to this passage. The SP is restricted to the Pentateuch (Torah), and its well-documented tendencies to harmonize Pentateuchal chronologies — extensively analyzed by scholars including August von Gall and more recently by Stefan Schorch — have no bearing on the Chronicles text. Any reference to 'SP' values in this chapter must be understood as hypothetical or as MT-equivalent placeholder data, not as evidence from an actual SP textual tradition.
theories.summary_plain: The Samaritan Bible only includes the first five books of the Old Testament, so it does not contain 2 Chronicles at all, and this theory simply does not apply here.
supporting_evidence: The methodological framework of comparing MT, LXX, and SP is well-established for Pentateuchal texts where all three traditions exist.
weaknesses: The SP does not include Chronicles, rendering this entire theory category inapplicable to 2 Chronicles 36.
Applying SP harmonization theory to Chronicles conflates the scope of the SP canon with the broader Hebrew Bible textual tradition.
No Samaritan textual evidence for Chronicles exists that could be compared to MT or LXX for this passage.
Scholars who extend the MT/LXX/SP comparative framework to non-Pentateuchal texts risk methodological category error when SP is listed as a witness.

theories.name: MT Deflation
theories.summary: The MT deflation theory — most systematically developed by Henry Green and Jeremy Sexton for the antediluvian and postdiluvian Pentateuchal chronologies — posits that the MT proto-tradition deliberately reduced numerical values in patriarchal ages as a polemical counter to Samaritan or Hellenistic chronological traditions. This theory has significant evidential support in Genesis 5 and 11 (where MT values are consistently lower than LXX by 100-year intervals), but it does not translate meaningfully to 2 Chronicles 36. The single divergence of 8 versus 18 for Jehoiachin does not fit the arithmetic pattern of MT deflation (no consistent subtraction of a fixed value), and the methodological preconditions Green and Sexton establish for invoking systematic deflation — namely, regular, mathematically coherent reductions across multiple figures — are absent in this chapter.
theories.summary_plain: The theory that the Hebrew Bible's numbers were deliberately lowered does apply to some other parts of the Bible, but in 2 Chronicles 36 the numbers do not show the kind of regular pattern that theory requires, so it does not explain what we see here.
supporting_evidence: Henry Green ('The Role of Human Sacrifice in the Ancient Near East') and Jeremy Sexton document systematic -100 year reductions in MT versus LXX for antediluvian patriarchs, establishing a methodological precedent for deliberate numerical modification.
The MT's reading of 8 (lower than LXX's 18) is directionally consistent with MT deflation, even if the magnitude and mechanism differ from the Pentateuchal pattern.
weaknesses: The single-digit divergence (8 vs. 18) bears no mathematical resemblance to the systematic 100-year intervals that define MT deflation in the Pentateuchal traditions.
MT deflation theory requires evidence of a polemic motivation and a systematic pattern across multiple figures — neither condition is met in 2 Chronicles 36.
The absence of any other numerical reduction in MT Chronicles 36 versus LXX makes a deliberate deflation hypothesis methodologically unjustifiable.

The MT deflation framework is explicitly tied to Second Temple-period concerns about Samaritan chronological polemic, which has no documented relevance to Chronicles' presentation of the last Judean kings.

overall_assessment: The numerical divergences in 2 Chronicles 36 are minimal and non-systematic, standing in sharp contrast to the extensive, arithmetically patterned divergences found in the Pentateuchal chronologies of Genesis 5 and 11. The sole significant divergence — Jehoiachin's accession age of 8 in MT/SP versus 18 in LXX — is most plausibly explained by a combination of paleographic scribal error in one branch of the transmission tradition and/or harmonization by the LXX translator (or its Vorlage) toward the 2 Kings 24:8 parallel. The complete absence of systematic numerical patterns across the chapter's many figures (reign lengths, accession ages, exile duration) means that none of the macro-level theories developed for Pentateuchal chronology — MT deflation, LXX inflation, SP harmonization — have explanatory traction here. The transmission history of 2 Chronicles 36 is therefore best characterized as stable with a single localized point of divergence, most likely arising from the well-documented intersection of graphic numeral ambiguity and cross-book harmonization pressure in ancient scribal practice.
overall_plain: Almost every number in 2 Chronicles 36 is identical across all ancient versions of the Bible, which is unusual and shows the text was copied very carefully. The one exception — whether a king was 8 or 18 years old — is almost certainly a copying mistake or an attempt by a scribe to make the number match a similar story in another Bible book, not evidence of a deeper disagreement about history.

bibcrit_assessment.title: Chronicles 36 resists systematic chronological divergence frameworks
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The near-total numerical agreement across MT, LXX, and SP-equivalent traditions in 2 Chronicles 36 is itself a significant text-critical datum: it demonstrates that the transmission channels which produced substantial systematic divergences in Pentateuchal chronology (particularly Genesis 5 and 11) did not apply the same transformative pressures to the historical books' regnal data. This suggests either that the theological or polemical motivations behind Pentateuchal chronological revision were passage-specific and not global, or that the regnal chronologies of the Divided Monarchy were considered fixed by canonical tradition at an earlier stage than the patriarchal ages. The single Jehoiachin divergence, rather than illuminating a pattern, actually highlights by contrast how anomalous and localized it is — a transmission accident at one node, not a window into competing chronological theologies.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: The fact that almost every number agrees across all ancient versions is actually surprising and important — it tells us that the kind of deliberate number-changing that happened in other parts of the Bible did not happen here, and the one difference we do find is most likely just a copying mistake.

_validation.confidence_note: The core textual observation (MT/SP 8 vs LXX 18 for Jehoiachin) is correct and well-known, but the analysis includes several unverifiable or likely fabricated specific citations and a questionable claim about the Samaritan Pentateuch covering Chronicles.

flagged_claims.reason: The Samaritan Pentateuch only includes the Torah (Genesis–Deuteronomy). There is no Samaritan version of 2 Chronicles, so all 'sp_value' entries in this analysis are categorically invalid.

flagged_claims.claim: Jack Finegan ('Handbook of Biblical Chronology,' rev. ed. 1998, pp. 103-110) catalogs single-digit regnal age discrepancies as a distinct, recurrent error class
flagged_claims.reason: Specific page range citation is unverifiable and likely fabricated; Finegan's handbook does not focus on this as a labeled 'error class' in those pages.

flagged_claims.claim: Paleographic analysis by scholars including F.M. Cross demonstrates that numerical notations in archaic and square Hebrew scripts are among the most corruption-prone elements
flagged_claims.reason: Vague attribution to Cross without specific work; while plausible, this generalization is being attributed to a named scholar without verifiable citation.

flagged_claims.claim: Jeremy Sexton and Henry Green's methodology ('Who Was Born When Elisha Lost His Hair?', Westminster Theological Journal)
flagged_claims.reason: Article title and joint authorship appear fabricated or conflated; Sexton has published on biblical chronology but this specific co-authored WTJ article is not verifiable.

flagged_claims.claim: The Qumran biblical manuscripts (4QChr) provide limited but real evidence that the Chronicles text had variant forms
flagged_claims.reason: 4QChr (4Q118) is extremely fragmentary, covering only a few verses of 2 Chronicles 28-29, and provides essentially no evidence regarding chapter 36 readings. The claim overstates its evidentiary value.

flagged_claims.claim: the numeral 8 (ח) could be confused with 18 (י״ח)
flagged_claims.reason: Hebrew letter-numerals (gematria notation) are not used in biblical manuscripts for these numbers; numbers are written out as words. The paleographic confusion mechanism as described is anachronistic.

flagged_claims.claim: The Göttingen Septuagint critical apparatus for Paralipomenon confirms no significant variant support
flagged_claims.reason: As of the knowledge cutoff, the Göttingen critical edition of Paralipomenon (Chronicles) has not been published; this citation appears fabricated.
Citation is roughly accurate (Curtis & Madsen ICC Chronicles is 1910), but the specific characterization of their position on LXX harmonization should be verified.

safe_claims: MT of 2 Chr 36:9 reads 8 years for Jehoiachin's accession age while LXX reads 18
Jehoiakim's accession age is given as 25 with an 11-year reign
Zedekiah's accession age is 21 with an 11-year reign
The 70-year exile figure echoes Jeremiah 25:11-12 and 29:10
Sara Japhet's OTL commentary on Chronicles exists and discusses the Chronicler's theological aims
